journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Editorial] Cancer consequences of the HIV funding crisis
abstract: Reductions in development assistance funding by previous major donors—the USA, the UK, France, and Germany—have led to substantial challenges to global HIV control in 2025. Against this stark backdrop, World AIDS Day 2025 was commemorated globally on Dec 1, 2025. UNAIDS released a report ahead of the day detailing the impact of the unprecedented changing international aid landscape on global HIV control programmes worldwide, particularly in low-income and middle-income countries. Failure to meet the 2030 global HIV targets could result in an additional 3·3 million new HIV infections between 2025 and 2030, according to the report.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Comment] Is PORTEC-4a the tipping point in endometrial cancer management?
abstract: The PORTEC-4a trial1 provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first prospective, randomised evidence that a molecular integrated risk profile can safely guide adjuvant therapy decisions in high-intermediate risk endometrial cancer, reinforcing the rationale for incorporating molecular classification into clinical practice. According to Anne Sophie V M van den Heerik and colleagues’ findings in the Lancet Oncology,2 a refined molecular stratification supports a more tailored adjuvant treatment, enabling either de-escalation or intensification of radiotherapy based on individual tumour biology.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Comment] Micrometastatic axillary disease after neoadjuvant treatment
abstract: In The Lancet Oncology, Giacomo Montagna and colleagues1 report the results of the large international retrospective OPBC-07/microNAC study, comparing the oncological outcomes and 3-year axillary recurrence rate for 1585 patients with breast cancer and residual micrometastases at axillary staging after neoadjuvant chemotherapy with and without completion axillary lymph node dissection (ALND). The feasibility and safety of axillary surgery de-escalation in patients with breast cancer who are at high risk of arm morbidity after ALND is an important clinical question.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Comment] The importance of preventing occupational cancer
abstract: Cancer is a leading cause of death globally, and the number of cancer cases is rising in most countries. This increase presents a substantial challenge for health systems across the globe, as extensive resources are required for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer patients.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Comment] Has the limit been reached in treatment of unresectable oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma?
abstract: SKYSCRAPER-08, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, marks a milestone in the treatment of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.1 Patients were randomly assigned to receive tiragolumab (a TIGIT inhibitor) plus atezolizumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor) and chemotherapy (paclitaxel and cisplatin) or to receive placebo and chemotherapy. Median progression-free survival was 6·2 months (95% CI 5·7–7·2) with tiragolumab plus atezolizumab versus 5·4 months (4·4–5·5) without (hazard ratio [HR] 0·56, 95% CI 0·45–0·70; p<0·0001), whereas median overall survival was 15·7 months (95% CI 13·3–20·4) versus 11·1 months (9·6–13·6; HR 0·70, 95% CI 0·55–0·88; p=0·0024).

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Comment] Artificial intelligence in pancreatic cancer detection: from premise to practice
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains among the deadliest cancers globally, primarily because symptoms typically appear at a late stage, resulting in diagnosis when curative treatment is no longer possible. Furthermore, detection of PDAC and other periampullary cancers on CT scans is challenging and requires specialised radiological expertise. However, even experienced radiologists miss early-stage tumours on CT scans; in a 2023 study, 15 expert radiologists achieved an average sensitivity of just 79·6% when reading contrast-enhanced CTs for PDAC.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Comment] The promise of scalable symptom surveillance with stepped collaborative care in oncology
abstract: Guidelines for managing deleterious symptoms from cancer and its treatments have been largely underused in practice. To address this problem, the National Cancer Institute launched the Improving the Management of Symptoms During and Following Cancer Treatment (IMPACT) consortium,1 an alliance of three research centres leading large-scale trials of electronic patient-reported outcome measure (ePROM) symptom surveillance and management systems. Andrea L Cheville and colleagues2 report findings from one IMPACT trial, showing positive effects of an enhanced, electronic health record (EHR)-facilitated cancer symptom control (E2C2) intervention on patients' and survivors' symptom burden and health-care use.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Comment] De-escalation of adjuvant radiotherapy in HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer
abstract: HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma has a distinct biology and responds favourably to primary radiation (and surgery)-based treatments. The long-term survival benefit is, however, offset by chronic detrimental impact on health-related quality of life for cancer survivors due to treatment-related toxic effects such as dysphagia and xerostomia. Consequently, many toxicity-mitigating de-escalation methods are being explored for HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma.1 Minimally invasive primary transoral surgery followed by de-intensification of post-operative (chemo) radiation depending on pathological risk assessment is one such investigational approach.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Comment] Retraction and republication—De-escalation of adjuvant radiotherapy in HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer
abstract: In September, 2025, The Lancet Oncology published results of the phase 3 MC1675 study on de-escalated adjuvant radiotherapy versus standard adjuvant treatment for human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.1 After publication, the corresponding author alerted us to numerical errors present in table 1 caused by a mistranscription of the number of patients in each category of nodal staging by AJCC 7th edition staging and AJCC 8th edition staging. These errors did not affect other data, findings, or interpretation in the paper and we have thus corrected the online version as of Dec 22, 2025.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Correspondence] The PREOPANC-2 trial in resectable and borderline resectable pancreatic cancer
abstract: The ESPAC1 and ESPAC1-Plus trials in 2001 and 2004 respectively established surgery and six months of adjuvant chemotherapy as the standard of care for empirically resectable pancreatic cancer. This protocol was confirmed repeatedly over the last 25 years, leading to an enormous increase in the volume of patients being treated with surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. The development of improved cancer treatment strategies requires that randomised controlled trials that aimed to be practice changing should include the best current standard of care as the control group.
authors: John P Neoptolemos, Christoph Springfeld, Daniel Öhlund, Markus W Büchler, Christoph W Michalski

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Correspondence] The PREOPANC-2 trial in resectable and borderline resectable pancreatic cancer
abstract: We congratulate Quisette P Janssen and colleagues on the phase 3 PREOPANC-2 trial.1 PREOPANC-2 was the successor of the phase 3 PREOPANC-1, which showed improved overall survival following pre-operative chemoradiotherapy and surgery versus surgery for patients with anatomically resectable or borderline resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. In light of the superiority for post-operative FOLFIRINOX versus gemcitabine and multiple rationales for pre-operative multi-agent chemotherapy, PREOPANC-2 tested the hypothesis that overall survival was longer following pre-operative FOLFIRINOX versus the gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy PREOPANC-1 approach.
authors: Alexander D Sherry, Krishan R Jethwa, Pavlos Msaouel, Ethan B Ludmir

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Correspondence] The PREOPANC-2 trial in resectable and borderline resectable pancreatic cancer – Authors' reply
abstract: We thank John P Neoptolemos and colleagues for their letter. They state that the ESPAC-1 trial set the standard of care for adjuvant therapy in resectable pancreatic cancer.1 However, ESPAC-1 set the standard of care for resected pancreatic cancer, including only those patients who had no occult metastases at surgery, underwent a resection, recovered from surgery, had no early recurrence, and remained fit for adjuvant treatment. In the adjuvant group of nine randomised controlled trials comparing neoadjuvant with adjuvant therapy, only 80% of all patients with resectable pancreatic cancer became patients with resected pancreatic cancer.

title: [News] Study links ultra-processed food consumption with bowel polyps in women younger than 50 years
abstract: New research by Andrew T Chan (Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA) and colleagues published in JAMA Oncology shows that younger women (aged ≤50 years) who eat the highest proportions of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) are at a 45% increased risk of developing bowel polyps that can later develop into colorectal cancer. UPFs are novel branded products made from inexpensive industrial ingredients such as hydrogenated oils, protein isolates or glucose or fructose syrup, and cosmetic food additives (including dyes, artificial sweeteners, and emulsifiers).

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [News] WHO sets new global standard for child‑friendly cancer drugs
abstract: On Nov 6, 2025, WHO published six new target product profiles for child‑friendly formulations of essential cancer medicines. The profiles aim to support the development of age‑appropriate formulations and close gaps in paediatric cancer care.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [News] Europe is falling behind on targets to address AMR
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is causing more than 35 000 deaths per year across Europe. According to estimates by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), based on 2024 data submitted by all countries in the EU and European Economic Area, Europe has met only one of five targets set to tackle the issue.

abstract: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, a public–private global health partnership with the goal of increasing access to immunisation in developing countries, is celebrating after working with lower-income countries to reach a key target to vaccinate millions of girls with the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine for cervical cancer in mid-November, 2025—6 weeks ahead of its original 3-year target.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [News] New South Wales expands cancer coverage for firefighters
abstract: On Nov 21, 2025, a ministerial media release announced a new legislation passed through Australian Parliament, expanding presumptive workers' compensation coverage for firefighters diagnosed with cancer. The new legislation extends the current list of 12 recognised malignancies in New South Wales, Australia, to include ten new cancers, including primary site lung, pancreatic, thyroid, and skin cancers. Reproductive cancers including cervical, ovarian, uterine, vaginal, vulval, and penile were also included.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [News] UK Government launches first Men's Health Strategy
abstract: On Nov 19, 2025, the UK Government launched the first Men's Health Strategy for England. The policy paper noted that, over the past decade, healthy life expectancy for men has fallen by 1·5 years and that men in parts of the country with the most poverty die on average 10 years earlier than men in parts with the least poverty. Men are more likely than women to smoke, drink alcohol, or use drugs, and be overweight or have obesity. 19% of deaths in men over 35 years are attributable to smoking, seven percentage points higher than women in the same age group, and 68% of deaths from liver disease are in men.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Perspectives] Current landscape, successes, and key challenges in cancer vaccine clinical trials across the UK
abstract: Cancer vaccines represent a transformative frontier in oncology, offering the potential to elicit durable and specific immune responses against tumour-associated or tumour-specific antigens. This technology has the potential to treat established malignancy, reduce tumour relapse, and even prevent cancer formation—improving survival outcomes. Advances in neoantigen discovery, mRNA vaccine platforms, and personalised immunotherapy have substantially enhanced the feasibility and efficacy of cancer vaccines across various malignancies.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Policy Review] A comprehensive framework for glioma surgery by the PIONEER Consortium and RANO resect group, part 1: intraoperative recommendations for mapping, monitoring, and decision making
abstract: In adult patients with newly diagnosed or recurrent diffuse glioma, more extensive resection is associated with longer progression-free and overall survival. Intraoperative mapping techniques are used to safely increase the extent of resection by locating, monitoring, and preserving the function of potentially infiltrated brain during surgery. However, there is no consensus on the indications for intraoperative mapping, the optimal functional tests to be used intraoperatively, or intraoperative decision making.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Policy Review] A comprehensive framework for glioma surgery by the PIONEER Consortium and RANO resect group, part 2: perioperative recommendations for neurological, language, functional, and quality-of-life assessment
abstract: Historically, the assessment of surgical outcomes in patients with glioma has been focused on technical outcomes, such as volumetric analysis of the residual tumour, progression-free survival, and overall survival. Other outcomes, such as neurological deficits, can be challenging to assess in an objective, quantifiable, and comprehensive manner. As a result, no consensus is available on methods to systematically evaluate perioperative neurological, language, cognitive, and functional outcomes in patients with glioma.

title: [Policy Review] International consensus recommendations and alignment of terminology for the histopathological diagnosis of extranodal extension in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: an HN-CLEAR initiative
abstract: Histopathologically detected extranodal extension leads to upstaging and treatment escalation in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. There is considerable variation in the prevalence of histopathologically detected extranodal extension in comparable studies. The Head and Neck Cancer International Group, which includes 23 organisations managing patients with head and neck cancer, identified several challenges in evaluating histopathologically detected extranodal extension. Thus, the Head and Neck Consensus Language for Ease and Reproducibility (HN-CLEAR) and its global stakeholders prioritised developing diagnostic criteria and uniform terminology for histopathologically detected extranodal extension.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Review] Development of a core outcome set for adolescents and young adults with cancer
abstract: Adolescents and young adults aged 15–39 years diagnosed with cancer are faced with unique challenges, which affect key developmental milestones and can create complex care needs. The aim of this study was to reach international consensus on the minimum set of outcomes to measure through the development of a core outcome set (COS). The COS development followed published methodological standards. A literature review and interviews with adolescents and young adults with cancer and health-care professionals generated a comprehensive list of 129 outcomes, spanning clinical and patient-reported outcomes relevant to adolescents and young adults with cancer.

journal: The Lancet Oncology
title: [Clinical Picture] High-output cardiac failure from a synovial sarcoma mimicking arteriovenous fistula
abstract: A 30-year-old woman presented to the Vascular Anomalies Centre at Shanghai Ninth People's Hospital in February, 2021, for a worsening and painful left inguinal arteriovenous fistula, which had been diagnosis 7 years previously following a strain 10 years ago. Initial endovascular embolisation in 2014 provided only transient relief, with subsequent symptom recurrence, progressive deep vein thrombosis, limb oedema, and claudication. By 2018, she had developed orthopnoea indicative of cardiac failure and required continuous diuretics, having received only symptomatic care until her presentation.
authors: Yuxi Chen, Jingwei Zhou, Hongyuan Liu, Xiaoxi Lin, Chen Hua

journal: The Lancet
title: [Editorial] The rise of China's research: a global opportunity
abstract: China has established itself as a global research superpower. Official data show that total research and development expenditure in 2024 exceeded 3·6 trillion yuan (roughly US$520 billion), up 8·3% from 2023, despite economic slowdowns, reflecting an unwavering commitment to science and technology from China. These investments have yielded tangible results: China published 878 300 papers in 2024 in the Web of Science Core Collection, up from just 26 200 in 2000, making it the world's most productive nation in terms of scientific publications.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Comment] National data for global 2030 targets for childhood cancer
abstract: While progress in childhood cancer outcomes has been tremendous, survival outcomes are notably lower for the majority of the world's children who live in low-income and middle-income countries.1–3 To address this disparity, the WHO Global Initiative for Childhood Cancer (GICC) was launched by WHO and St Jude Children's Research Hospital with global partners at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in 2018. The GICC targets a 5-year overall survival of at least 60% globally by 2030 while reducing suffering, through a systems-wide approach known as CureAll.
authors: Catherine G Lam, Scott C Howard

journal: The Lancet
title: [Comment] Fetal and maternal outcomes following mpox infection in pregnancy
abstract: Pregnant women are at high risk of severe mpox due to the immunological and hormonal changes that occur in pregnancy.1,2 Available evidence suggests that monkeypox virus (MPXV) clade I is associated with more clinically significant, adverse pregnancy outcomes, as well as vertical transmission, than clade II.3 The first probable case of MPXV clade I in pregnancy was reported in DR Congo in 1988: a woman aged 44 years had preterm birth of a female neonate with generalised skin rashes consistent with mpox at around 7 months of pregnancy.
authors: Akaninyene Eseme Ubom, Sebastine Oseghae Oiwoh

journal: The Lancet
title: [Comment] Health equity and displaced people: challenges, progress, and the path forward
abstract: In 2024, more than 123 million people were forcibly displaced worldwide, driven largely by conflicts, persecutions, and human rights violations.1 Displaced populations include refugees (people who flee their country due to conflict or persecution), internally displaced people (those forced to flee their homes but who remain within their country's borders), and undocumented migrants and asylum seekers (individuals who cross borders without formal legal status, including those awaiting a decision on their protection claim).
authors: Davidi Tawfiles, Mohamed Reyad Zughbur, William E Rosa, Edward Christopher Dee, Mohja Marhoom, Nahla Gafer, Ophira Ginsburg, Fouad M Fouad, Richard Sullivan

journal: The Lancet
title: [Comment] Parkinson's disease: emerging opportunities through global collaboration
abstract: Precision medicine holds enormous promise in enhancing treatment efficacy and advancing therapeutic development, leading to more equitable care. However, to realise this promise in all individuals with Parkinson's disease, the disease needs to be understood in populations other than those traditionally studied. Pursuing this approach has many rewards. The identification of a GBA1 risk factor for Parkinson's disease in west Africa in 2023, through a global collaboration, is a clear example.1 GBA1 is a common risk factor, present in more than 40% of patients with Parkinson's disease from Nigeria.
authors: Andrew Singleton, Cornelis Blauwendraat, Huw R Morris, Alastair J Noyce, Christine Klein, Ignacio Mata, Njideka Okubadejo, Maria Teresa Periñan, Lana M Chahine

journal: The Lancet
title: [Comment] The Lancet MedZero: carbon analytics for health care, by health care, at scale
abstract: All 10 of the hottest years on record occurred in the past decade, with 2024 exceeding the 1·5°C Paris Agreement commitment.1 The Lancet and WHO agree: “climate change is the biggest threat to global health in the 21st century”.2 Health professionals are responding to this medical emergency. Royal colleges and national health-care associations are developing low-carbon clinical guidelines; 102 world-leading academic institutions contribute to the Lancet Countdown;3 and efforts such as the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine Pathfinder Initiative4 and a forthcoming Lancet Commission on sustainable health care5 are charting a path forward.
authors: Nick Watts, Thomas Andrew, Jessamy Bagenal, Matthew J Eckelman, Jacob Fry, Agnes Henson, Richard Horton, Wanrudee Isaranuwatchai, Slava Jankin, Sarin KC, Jonathan T E Lee, Scott McAlister, Forbes McGain, Keisuke Nansai, Catherine O'Shea, Lydia Tang, Michelle Tan Bee Hua, Chantelle Rizan

journal: The Lancet
title: [Comment] Offline: Information—crisis, what crisis?
abstract: I suggested last week that Filipino journalist Maria Ressa (Nobel Peace Laureate, 2021) is a good place to start if you are seeking a guide to political advocacy for health. Her book How to Stand Up to a Dictator (2022) is a memoir, but so much more. Another writer receiving a great deal of attention (in the UK, at least) is Naomi Alderman and her book Don’t Burn Anyone at the Stake Today (2025). Alderman is a classical scholar, novelist, and broadcaster. Although Ressa and Alderman write from different perspectives, their targets coincide.

journal: The Lancet
title: [World Report] Trump announces withdrawal from 66 global organisations
abstract: Several health-related organisations are targeted by the USA's announcement, although the details of how withdrawal will work in practice are unclear. Faith McLellan reports.

journal: The Lancet
title: [World Report] Ceasefire barely improves “horrific” situation in Gaza
abstract: Two new reports detail the harm being done to women's and children's health. Sharmila Devi reports.

journal: The Lancet
title: [World Report] Research focus: the Fleming Initiative
abstract: A collaboration based at Imperial College London aims to find multidisciplinary solutions to the growing health issue of antimicrobial resistance. Sharmila Devi reports.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Perspectives] In search of rest—Kerry James Marshall: The Histories
abstract: Like many academics, I once wrote a paper I never submitted. It seemed beyond the acceptability of every mainstream academic health journal I have encountered. The title was “They shoot Black intellectuals, don't they”. In it, I reflected on what it meant to be a Black scholar, working in the wake of many who spoke on the interconnectedness of Black life, health, and the wider political order—and who eventually found themselves on the receiving end of the murderous gaze of violence and erasure.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Perspectives] Dengue and the urban condition: a historical reckoning
abstract: Randall M Packard's Fevered Cities: A History of Dengue Epidemics offers a compelling and nuanced examination of dengue fever, situating this pervasive disease within the intricate fabric of urban environments and global socio-ecological transformations. Packard, Emeritus Professor of the History of Medicine at Johns Hopkins University, presents dengue as far more than a mere biomedical condition, framing it instead as a product of complex interactions among ecological, social, political, and climatic factors.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Perspectives] Linguistic pragmatism: a woman with progressive abdominal pain in Thailand
abstract: Misa, a 75-year-old Akha-speaking woman, presented to the emergency department of a public hospital in northern Thailand with several weeks of progressive abdominal pain. Unlike many people of Akha descent in Thailand, Misa lived in a physically accessible village and had a Thai identity card that gave her access to Thailand's universal health-care system. Misa's children were away, so she was brought to the hospital by an acquaintance. Misa was seen by Dr Ann, an emergency physician of northern Thai ethnicity.
authors: Scott Stonington, Preeyanoot Surinkaew, Thidathit Prachanukool

journal: The Lancet
title: [Obituary] Terence English
abstract: Cardiothoracic surgeon who did the UK's first successful heart transplantation. He was born in Pietermaritzburg, South Africa, on Oct 3, 1932, and died at home in Iffley, Oxford, UK, on Nov 23, 2025, aged 93 years.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] A risky rollback on hepatitis B birth dose in the USA
abstract: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has voted eight to three to withdraw the long-standing recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants born to mothers who test hepatitis B virus-negative, instead recommending shared clinical decision making and delaying the first dose to no earlier than 2 months for those not vaccinated at birth.1 This decision is a departure from evidence-grounded immunisation policy and should not be implemented without a transparent rationale and a credible plan to prevent predictable implementation failures.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] Ebola and health-care providers: the case for preventive vaccination
abstract: The sixteenth Ebola virus disease outbreak declared on Sept 4, 2025, in Bulape Health Zone, DR Congo, underscores the persistent vulnerability of health-care providers during the onset of epidemics.1
authors: Jean-Pierre Van geertruyden, Ynke Larivière, Trésor Zola Matuvanga, Pierre Van Damme, Hypolite Muhindo Mavoko

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] The UK COVID-19 Inquiry and the next pandemic
abstract: The second report of the UK COVID-19 Inquiry1 fails to discuss what resources should be established and maintained to control a future pandemic. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the reproductive rate of SARS-CoV-2 increased as more infectious variants evolved, but it could have been reduced to less than 1 if weekly testing of the whole population and quarantining of infected households had been available at the outset,2 with the aim of avoiding lockdown and greatly reducing mortality. This strategy was belatedly accepted by the UK Government, which announced Operation Moonshot3 in September, 2020, but failed to implement the key element: the use of generic test reagents in local NHS laboratories.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] Closing the prevention gap in heart failure: World Heart Federation
abstract: Heart failure is a complex clinical syndrome that represents the final common pathway for most cardiovascular diseases. It is also a major contributor to mortality, disability, and rising health-care costs. Despite a dramatic decline in age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs) for most cardiovascular diseases globally since the 1970s, the ASMR for heart failure has remained largely unchanged or has even increased in some regions. For example, from 1970 to 2022, in the USA, the ASMR declined by 89% for acute myocardial infarction, 81% for ischaemic heart disease, and 66% for all heart disease combined; however, it increased 146% for heart failure.
authors: George A Mensah, Dorairaj Prabhakaran, Amam C Mbakwem, Jagat Narula

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] A call for equity in organ transplantation for people with HIV
abstract: The Lancet Series on solid organ transplantation is a timely call to advance global equity and highlights the importance of ensuring those who might benefit from solid organ transplantation have fair and just access. Although the authors describe numerous obstacles to solid organ transplantation, people with HIV face unique and intersecting barriers, despite improvements in life expectancy with antiretroviral therapy (ART).1 Equity in solid organ transplantation for people with HIV is essential to achieve the UNAIDS fourth 90 target, which aims to optimise health-related quality of life and healthy longevity for people with HIV.
authors: David W J Griffin, James H McMahon, Jennifer F Hoy

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] Interpreting the pT1 subgroup in the ASTER 70s trial
abstract: The ASTER 70s trial by Etienne Brain and colleagues1 is a landmark phase 3 study redefining treatment strategy in older women (aged ≥70 years) with oestrogen receptor-positive, HER2 (also known as ERBB2)-negative breast cancer. However, buried within the overall non-significant result is a noteworthy subgroup signal: in patients with pT1 tumours, the chemotherapy group had an 8-year overall survival of 76·7% compared with 84·5% in the hormonotherapy-alone group, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0·51 (95% CI 0·27–0·96), suggesting a potential treatment effect that is contrary to traditional staging logic.
authors: Huichuan Tian, Yaoyao Bian, Deyao Zhang

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] Interpreting the pT1 subgroup in the ASTER 70s trial – Authors' reply
abstract: We thank Huichuan Tian and colleagues for their insightful commentary on the ASTER 70s trial.1 We remind readers that this study selected women aged 70 years and older who had undergone surgery for oestrogen receptor-positive, HER2 (also known as ERBB2)-negative breast cancer and were considered at high-risk due to a high genomic grade index (GGI) of the tumour, regardless of any other inclusion criteria. These patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to chemotherapy followed by hormonotherapy or hormonotherapy alone.
authors: Etienne Brain, Florence Rollot-Trad, Telma Roques, Julie Henriques, Dewi Vernerey

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] Health-care professions’ silent complicity in Palestine's health crisis
abstract: The Lancet's Oct 4, 2025, cover cites a Correspondence1 on Gaza by Alessandro Vitale and colleagues, which states “Staying silent while pretending to be neutral is in effect, a form of complicity”. Institutions have not simply remained silent—many actively silence those who speak, while maintaining investments and partnerships that materially sustain the destruction of health in Palestine.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] Health-care professions’ silent complicity in Palestine's health crisis
abstract: Recent Correspondence1 has again foregrounded the complicit silence among medical and surgical societies worldwide in the face of Gaza's ongoing healthocide, including the deliberate targeting of health-care workers.1 This shameful inaction is mirrored across health-care professional associations.
authors: Hiba Zafran, Karen Whalley Hammell, Moussa Abumostafa, Pier-Luc Turcotte, Tal Jarus

journal: The Lancet
title: [Correspondence] Health-care professions’ silent complicity in Palestine's health crisis – Authors' reply

journal: The Lancet
title: [Articles] Abluminus DES+ sirolimus-eluting stent versus everolimus-eluting stent in patients with diabetes and coronary artery disease (ABILITY Diabetes Global): results from a multicentre, randomised controlled trial
abstract: In patients with diabetes undergoing PCI, the Abluminus DES+ SES was not non-inferior to the XIENCE EES, resulting in higher rates of ischaemia-driven target-lesion revascularisation and target lesion failure at 12-month follow-up. Event rates between 12 and 24 months were similar between groups. These findings highlight the persistent challenge of optimising outcomes in patients with diabetes and underscore the need for continued innovation in stent design and adjunctive pharmacotherapy to reduce residual ischaemic risk in this population.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Articles] Socioeconomic inequalities in cancer survival and access to health care among children and adolescents in China, 2018–24: a prospective nationwide cohort study
abstract: China has achieved major progress in childhood cancer survival, but inequalities remain across and within regions at different levels of socioeconomic development. The level of inequality appears greater among adolescents. While interprovincial health-care seeking was generally associated with higher survival, disparities in outcomes persisted, aligned with the socioeconomic development of patients' residence and treatment locations. Tiered resource allocation for paediatric cancer care at provincial and regional levels should be prioritised in China's health system to advance health equity.

journal: The Lancet
title: [Articles] Maternal and neonatal outcomes after infection with monkeypox virus clade I during pregnancy in DR Congo: a pooled, prospective cohort study

journal: JAMA Current Issue
title: Doors
abstract: Even though my drug isn’t chemo, the infusion is at the Cancer Center. Here, self-pity becomes a Bangalorean house lizard, scuttles off quickly, quietly. I pass the empty front desk, sit in Bay B, look out across the sea of printed headscarves—daisies, pink ribbons, dancing bananas. I watch grapes passed between a woman’s gauze-wrapped hand and the supple, tattooed fingers of her caretaker, around my age, perhaps her daughter, who chews the purple flesh, her eyes on the too-bright garden beds out the window, ignoring the NO FOOD sign on the door. It yawns open and the woman, with forbidden sweet balled in her cheek, smooths her shirt as her daughter brushes loose strands: a practiced, prom-like readying, her spine straight all the way inside. They disappear one by one—daisy scarf, 49ers shirt, crochet hooks with a walker— until the magazines grow quiet and only the warm dents of rumps are left with me. Sensing I’m alone, the lizard peers in again, momentarily. The door clicks and a medical assistant attempts my name until I relieve him of his struggling. But I’m struggling to realize there is no separate entrance for nononcology patients. That we all walk in and out the same door.

journal: JAMA Current Issue
title: Illness and Poetry as Portals to Shared Experience
abstract: As the literary critic Anatole Broyard proclaimed in his memoir Intoxicated by My Illness: And Other Writings on Life and Death, “Illness is not just an individual experience, it is a social one. It is one of the few things we all share, the experience of our own frailty.” In “Doors,” poetry acts as a parallel portal into universal human experience. The poem’s title first suggests this fruitful comparison between poetry and illness. The speaker of the poem then goes on to locate us alongside her in an infusion center, where “Even though my drug isn’t chemo,” together we “look out across the sea/of printed headscarves—daisies, pink ribbons,/dancing bananas,” the diversity of humanity illustrated by the multitude of designs that swaddle the bald heads of fellow patients. Thus poetry affirms all are implicitly united in the experience of illness, whether it be cancer, the speaker’s unnamed condition, or whatever may befall us on our own journeys. Dismissing the creeping “Bangalorean house lizard” of her own self-pity becomes possible as she finds comforting solidarity despite her eventual aloneness as the treatment recipients “disappear/one by one…the magazines grow quiet/and only the warm dents of rumps/are left with me” (tragicomically reminding us, also, of our shared mortality). In the end, the speaker remains transfixed by the threshold across which she, and we all, must cross. “…I’m struggling/to realize there is no separate entrance/for nononcology patients,” she keenly observes, “That we all walk in and out/the same door.”

abstract: To the Editor In a Perspective article, Drs Blumenthal and Galvin provided a valuable taxonomy of marketization, commercialization, corporatization, and financialization in US health care. The challenge for the US system is not whether to accept or reject these market-driven forces but how to structure and govern them. They are best understood as neutral forces whose effects, harmful or beneficial, depend on design and oversight. Experience from other high-income health care systems shows that, when paired with robust regulatory frameworks, market incentives can enhance patient choice, support clinician autonomy, and sustain quality improvements.

abstract: To the Editor As radiation oncologists specializing in skin and soft tissue malignancies, we appreciated the Review on cutaneous melanoma by Dr Joshi and colleagues. However, we were surprised to note that radiotherapy was not mentioned. Thus, we thought it important to remind the melanoma clinical community of the phase 3 ANZMTG/TROG 02.01 randomized clinical trial, which enrolled 250 patients with high-risk clinically involved lymph node disease at 16 centers and reported that adjuvant nodal radiation therapy decreased in-field nodal recurrence (hazard ratio, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.33-0.89). The 5-year cumulative incidence of lymph node field relapse as a first site of relapse was 18% with adjuvant radiotherapy vs 33% with observation (P = .01), and the 5-year cumulative incidence for isolated lymph node field relapse as a site of first relapse was 8% with adjuvant radiotherapy vs 23% with observation (P = .002).

journal: JAMA Current Issue

journal: JAMA Current Issue
title: Toripalimab-Based Therapy Without Concurrent Cisplatin for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma—Reply
abstract: In Reply We thank Drs Altınışık İnan and Guo for their correspondence, which provides an opportunity to clarify aspects of the DIAMOND study in NPC. Although the standard therapy evaluated in the study was not incorporated into clinical guidelines when enrollment began in August 2021, evidence supporting this approach had already emerged. Specifically, the CONTINUUM trial, completed in March 2020 in the same target population, demonstrated the efficacy of combining programmed cell death protein1 (PD-1) blockade with induction-concurrent chemoradiotherapy in locoregionally advanced NPC. This regimen has since been endorsed by the 2024 Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology guidelines for high-risk patients with locoregionally advanced NPC (T4N1M0 or T1-4N2-3M0), although it has not yet been established as an international standard of care. Moreover, all clinical trials cited in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines for head and neck cancers that recommend concurrent cisplatin for NPC used a dosing schedule of 100 mg/m2 every 3 weeks. Although weekly cisplatin (30-40 mg/m2) is an option for clinical practice, supporting evidence remains limited, and it has not been widely adopted in pivotal trials. We concur that data on immune-related adverse events are crucial; however, due to space constraints, these results were presented in eTable 11 of the article’s Supplement 2 rather than in the main text.

title: Broader Adoption of SGLT2 Inhibitors in Clinical Practice
abstract: Over the past decade, the indications for sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors for kidney and cardiovascular risk reduction have expanded, driven by clinical trial evidence demonstrating their efficacy among individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD), heart failure, diabetes, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Current clinical practice guidelines for people with CKD recommend their use for individuals with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) greater than or equal to 20 mL/min/1.73 m2 who also have type 2 diabetes, heart failure, or a urine albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) greater than 200 mg/g. A major unanswered question is whether SGLT2 inhibitors would improve kidney outcomes among those with lower degrees of albuminuria or more advanced CKD than recommended by current guidelines. To address this crucial knowledge gap, the SGLT2 Inhibitor Meta-Analysis Cardio-Renal Trialists’ Consortium (SMART-C) conducted 2 companion meta-analyses of randomized placebo-controlled SGLT2 inhibitor trials to assess the effect on kidney outcomes among key subgroups of patients and report their results in this issue of JAMA.

These data provide valuable insights into the burden of metastatic disease among adolescents and young adults with cancer and identify cancer types for which adolescents and young adults face high risk for metastatic recurrence and associated mortality. journal: JAMA Oncology Current Issue
title: Clarifying End Point Definitions, Missingness, and Covariate Balance in the International TNT Study—Reply
abstract: In Reply We thank Zhu and Wang for their interest in the International TNT Study. In our series, 12.1% of patients were offered a watch and wait strategy, and 31.9% of these had salvage surgery for local regrowth, which occurred at a median of 34 (IQR, 24-46) weeks after treatment completion. In only 1.7% and 22.0% of the cases, respectively, local regrowth was accompanied or followed by tumor progression/recurrence elsewhere. While increasingly offered in clinical practice, nonoperative management mostly remains an opportunistic strategy for select patients rather than a planned approach primarily aiming at organ preservation. Accordingly, if followed by an R0/R1 salvage surgery, isolated local regrowth during watch and wait suggests failure of complete response assessment rather than treatment failure and true recurrence after a curative-intent strategy. In line with international consensus recommendations, we excluded isolated, R0/R1 resected, local regrowth during watch and wait from the censoring events for either local progression or event-free survival (EFS), and we do not share the concerns about this handling underestimating local events and inflating EFS. Regarding multiple imputation for missing data, we did acknowledge this as a limitation of our study. Notably, the proportion of patients with no available information for each prognostic variable was reported, overall and by treatment regimen, in the supplementary material. Of the 61.2% of patients tested for mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR)/microsatellite instability (MSI-H), 3.6% had dMMR/MSI-H tumors. Collecting information on the subsequent use of immune checkpoint inhibitors on disease progression was out of scope. Outcomes of our TNT-treated population by mismatch repair/microsatellite status will be reported in a separate article. We agree that covariate balance diagnostics after propensity vector matching are informative. Balance before matching can be assessed from the table in the manuscript. We assessed postmatching balance for categorical baseline variables by computing the proportion in each group at each level of the variable, then computing the absolute between-group difference in proportions for each pair of groups. For age at diagnosis, we compared means and 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles across groups. The largest differences in proportions were observed for cN stage; cN2 was disproportionately represented in the RAPIDO-like and OPRA induction-like groups (52% and 53%, respectively) relative to the PRODIGE23-like (33%) and OPRA consolidation-like groups (41%), while cN1 disproportionately represented in the RAPIDO-like group relative to the PRODIGE23-like group (37% vs 52%). The next largest difference observed was in low tumor grade between the PRODIGE23-like and OPRA induction-like groups (42% vs 28%). All other differences were 11 percentage points or fewer. For age at diagnosis, the maximum between-group differences in the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles were 2, 3.5, and 3 years, respectively. Finally, regarding the maturity of survival estimates, we agree that the similarity of results across treatment regimens should be interpreted cautiously, and this is the reason why we emphasized 3-year rather than 5-year EFS and overall survival probabilities in the article. We do not think that interpretation would be improved by using restricted mean survival times that are less intuitive for clinicians despite their worth in settings marked by nonproportional hazards, which does not appear to be the case in our study.

abstract: In Reply In the ACHIEVE study, 2 patients (3.2%) discontinued treatment due to grade 2 pneumonia. Both were never-smoking women with L858R-mutated adenocarcinoma. The first patient, a woman aged 57 years with stage IVA disease, developed chest tightness after physical activity. Radiologic examinations revealed scattered inflammatory opacities. Differential diagnosis suggested a high probability of drug-related interstitial lung disease (ILD). This event occurred 137 days after initiation of tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy and resolved within 20 days with oral prednisone administration. The second patient was a woman aged 73 years with stage IVB disease who presented with chest tightness and shortness of breath after physical activity. Based on imaging and medical history, ILD was the primary diagnostic consideration. This ILD event occurred 202 days after initiation of targeted therapy. Following prednisone administration, her pneumonia improved to grade 1 by week 2 and resolved completely by week 5. To ensure patient safety, the study protocol stipulates in the treatment discontinuation section (Protocol 7.8.1, line 843) that patients who develop interstitial pneumonia should permanently discontinue study treatment. In accordance with protocol requirement, treatment was permanently discontinued and both patients were withdrawn from the study, even though the ILD had recovered in both cases.

The trial enrolled 52 patients across 17 tumor types, with endometrial cancer comprising half of the cohort. Half of the patients were treatment naive, and half had received 1 prior line of therapy; only 1 had prior exposure to checkpoint inhibition. The overall objective response rate was 63%, including 5 complete responses. An additional 8 patients achieved stable disease, yielding a disease control rate of 79%. Eleven patients experienced progression, either clinically before the first imaging or at first imaging assessment. Responses were similar between treatment-naive and previously treated patients, and 20 of 26 patients with endometrial cancer achieved disease control. Immune-related adverse events were common, occurring in 75% of patients, with 23% experiencing grade 3 or higher toxicity.

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has generated remarkable enthusiasm in medicine, and otolaryngology is no exception. Yet current literature remains limited in scope and quality, dominated by feasibility studies using single-institution, internally validated datasets. Without a shift in direction, early excitement may collapse into unmet expectations. In this issue of JAMA Otolaryngology−Head & Neck Surgery, Novi et al highlight the innovation and promise of AI and deep learning (DL) in otolaryngology, a field rich in data, from endoscopy and microscopy to electrophysiology. They also underscore the growing chasm between proof-of-concept studies and applications meaningfully improving patient care. Since its approval, BSD has been used as a stand-alone procedure with or without general anesthesia, as well as part of a hybrid procedure in conjunction with endoscopic sinus surgery. Interestingly, the explosion of BSD use has not decreased the amount of endoscopic sinus surgeries performed annually. According to recent clinical consensus statements, BSD may be used for limited chronic paranasal sinus disease and in cases of recurrent acute rhinosinusitis and is not indicated for management of headache or obstructive sleep apnea or in cases of absent pathology on computed tomography (CT) or imaging.

abstract: To the Editor I read with great interest the recent study by Du et al, “Updated Thresholds of Basal Calcitonin Level and Extent of Lymph Node Metastasis in Initially Treated Medullary Thyroid Cancer,” and the accompanying Invited Commentary. However, the results reported in Table 2 appear internally inconsistent, possibly due to transposing of the sensitivity and specificity columns for American Thyroid Association (ATA) serum calcitonin thresholds of 20, 50, and 500 pg/mL (to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 0.292); however, for 200 pg/mL, they seem correct. The ATA thresholds were originally chosen to minimize the false negative rate. In this context, the reported very low sensitivity for the 50 pg/mL cutoff—implying a very high false negative rate—is implausible, as is the correspondingly very high specificity; the same applies for the cutoff values of 50 and 500 pg/mL.

journal: JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery Current Issue
title: Updated Calcitonin Thresholds More Accurately Predict Lymph Node Metastasis?—Reply
abstract: In Reply We thank Colli for his thoughtful comments on our study. We would like to provide a detailed clarification to address what we believe a misunderstanding regarding our updated thresholds. First, we fully agree that the ATA thresholds seek to minimize missed LNMs by adopting very low preoperative calcitonin cutoffs. However, this inevitably leads to an extremely high rate of overtreatment, resulting in unnecessary complications and surgical morbidity. For example, under the current cutoffs, patients newly diagnosed with medullary thyroid cancer and with preoperative calcitonin greater than 20 pg/mL would be considered for lateral neck dissection. In our data, patients with calcitonin levels of 20 to 50 pg/mL had 5-year structural recurrence-free survival rates of 92.1% and 100% in the training and validation cohorts, respectively, with no recurrences observed in the validation cohort, comparable to 92.7% and 93.0% in the 241.9 to 693.9 pg/mL group. Thus, prophylactic neck dissection in patients with calcitonin levels of 20 to 50 pg/mL would likely lead to substantial overtreatment.

abstract: In Reply We thank Nafiu for her letter, which raised 3 thoughtful points for response. First, our study adhered to the standard of care, in which patients are treated by appropriate specialists based on their presenting symptoms. We respectfully but firmly reject the assertion that we omitted crucial comparisons of key clinical factors that guided treatment. As explained in the Methods of our article, infants were included based on a presentation of stridor, aspiration, apnea, or failure to thrive. As qualified airway specialists, the decision to treat patients is based on the flexible endoscopic evaluations for respiratory symptoms and airway inflammation, so these factors were not omitted. Additionally, clinical signs of stridor or aspiration were explicitly evaluated in conjunction with weight, prematurity, and other factors. The concern that this patient population was not randomized leads to confusion on our part, as true randomization is not possible in a retrospective cohort study because randomization requires actively assigning participants to groups. The standard of care for managing laryngomalacia dictates that patients are treated by appropriate physicians for their symptoms, whether airway (otolaryngology) or acid reflux (pediatrics/gastroenterology), and these standards were not altered for the sake of randomization.
